article.title: Why a High Conversion Rate Can Hide a Shrinking Opportunity
article.why: Read conversion rates together with their denominator and absolute outcomes.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: Background: conversion funnels and rate interpretation

paragraphs.en:
A rising conversion rate usually sounds like good news. If a campaign converts 5 percent of eligible customers this month compared with 4 percent last month, the natural conclusion is that performance improved. But a rate is a ratio. It tells us what share of a denominator converted; it does not tell us whether the denominator itself became larger or smaller.

Suppose a business had 100,000 eligible customers and a 4 percent conversion rate. That produces 4,000 conversions. The next month, stricter eligibility rules reduce the audience to 60,000, while better targeting raises conversion to 5 percent. The dashboard shows a one-point improvement, yet the business gets only 3,000 conversions. Efficiency improved inside the remaining audience, but the total opportunity shrank enough to reduce the final result.

This distinction matters whenever the denominator can change. Website traffic can fall while checkout conversion rises. A sales team can qualify fewer leads while its win rate improves. A credit campaign can narrow eligibility and report a stronger response rate. In each case, the rate may improve partly because the population became easier to convert.

Analysts should therefore report at least three numbers together: the eligible population or traffic volume, the conversion rate, and the absolute number of conversions. Revenue or profit may be a fourth layer because not every conversion has the same economic value. A useful decomposition is: conversions equal eligible population multiplied by conversion rate. This simple identity forces the discussion to include both scale and efficiency.

Segment composition also matters. Imagine that low-propensity customers disappear from the denominator because of a policy change. The overall conversion rate can rise even if no segment improves. That is a composition effect, not necessarily evidence that marketing became more persuasive. Comparing stable segments or a common customer population can help separate these explanations.

The same logic applies to experiments and machine-learning targeting. A model may produce a high CVR by selecting only the easiest customers, but the business may care about incremental conversions across a larger population. A top-score strategy should therefore be evaluated against capacity, treatment cost, incremental lift, and the size of the addressable audience, not CVR alone.

When presenting results, avoid saying only, ‘CVR improved from 4 to 5 percent.’ A stronger statement is, ‘CVR improved by one percentage point, but the eligible audience fell 40 percent, so conversions declined from 4,000 to 3,000.’ That sentence distinguishes efficiency from opportunity size. A good rate is useful, but a business ultimately acts on people, transactions, revenue, and profit—not percentages in isolation.
paragraphs.zh: CVR 上升不一定代表最終業務成果增加。轉換數＝eligible population × conversion rate；如果分母大幅縮小，即使率改善，轉換件數仍可能下降。還要注意分母構成改變造成的 composition effect。報告時應把母數、CVR、轉換件數，必要時再加收入或利潤一起呈現。
paragraphs.ja: CVRの上昇だけでは業績改善とは言えません。コンバージョン件数は対象母数×CVRで決まるため、対象者が大幅に減れば率が改善しても件数は減少します。また、低確率層が母数から外れただけで全体CVRが上がる構成効果にも注意が必要です。母数・率・件数をセットで報告することが重要です。

vocabulary.usage: Always inspect the denominator behind a rate.
Absolute conversions can fall while CVR rises.
The rate increase may be a composition effect.
Measure the size of the addressable audience.
The business cares about incremental conversions.
Use decomposition to separate scale from efficiency.

phrases.explanation: 區分效率指標與絕對規模。

grammar.title: while + clause
grammar.body: 用來對比同時發生的兩個方向，例如 traffic fell while conversion rose.

business.term: The rate improved, but the denominator contracted.
business.explanation: 簡潔說明率改善但機會規模縮小。
business.example: The rate improved, but the denominator contracted by 40%.

business.term: Let’s look at the absolute number as well.
business.example: CVR is up; let’s look at the absolute number as well.

quiz.question: Can conversions fall when CVR rises?
quiz.answer: Yes. If the eligible population shrinks enough, absolute conversions can decline despite a higher rate.
